title: Find a Standard Regression Equation from Data
description: Turn information from a table, graph, or word problem into points, enter the points in a Desmos table, and use the Regression button to fit a linear, quadratic, or exponential equation.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep what you tried, even if you got stuck. You can continue without submitting an answer.

shared_prompt.title: Quadratic height model
shared_prompt.html:
A quadratic function \(H(t)=at^2+bt+c\) models a plant’s height, in centimeters, \(t\) weeks after observation began.

Plant height observations
\(t\)\(H(t)\)
19.5
313.5
642
876

What is the value of \(a\)?

blocks.html:
Let the data build the equation

The opening table has uneven time steps and three missing coefficients. Finding them by hand would mean connecting several equations.

Regression lets Desmos fit an equation to the points. We’ll start with three simple points so you can learn the table controls, then return to the plant data.

content.title: Start with three points
content.instructions_html: Choose Add Item (+) → Table. Enter the three shared points, with inputs on the left. Click the Regression button beside the table values and keep Linear. Read its equation.

feedback.success_message_html: Nice work! The linear regression fits these three points. Read the equation Desmos displays.
feedback.retry_message_html: Not yet. Check the table rows, the regression row, and the model against the problem, then submit again.

targeted_hints.message_html: Enter the three points with Add Item (+) → Table, one row at a time.
The table does not hold the required rows yet. Re-check each value against the problem.
With the table filled, click the small regression button beside the table values (a line with four scatterplot dots).

feedback.solution_html: Table rows \((0,2)\), \((1,5)\), \((2,8)\), then the Regression button with the model set to Linear.

figure.alt: A Desmos table with an arrow pointing to the Regression button beside it, shown as a fitted line with four scatterplot dots
figure.caption: The Regression button sits beside the table values.

content.prompt: Which equation did the linear regression produce for the points \((0,2)\), \((1,5)\), and \((2,8)\)?
content.hint: Look at the equation displayed beside the table — Desmos already built it. To confirm, test the displayed equation against any one of the three points.
content.explanation: Desmos displays \(y=3x+2\), which matches all three points. You entered the data; the Regression button built the equation.

blocks.html:
Keep input first, output second

Each row, marked point, or statement gives a pair \((\text{input},\text{output})\). Put inputs in the table’s left column and outputs in its right column.

“After 2 hours, there are 180 bacteria” becomes \((2,180)\).

content.prompt: A graph marks the points \((-2,7)\), \((0,3)\), and \((4,-5)\). How should those data be entered in a Desmos table?
choices: Enter only the three y-values because the graph supplies x.
Enter \(7,3,-5\) in the left column and \(-2,0,4\) in the right column.
Enter the equation of the graph instead of using a table.
Enter \(-2,0,4\) in the left column and \(7,3,-5\) in the right column.
content.hint: The first coordinate is the input and belongs in the left column. The second coordinate is the output.
content.explanation: Keep each ordered pair together: x-values on the left and their matching y-values on the right.

blocks.html:
Read the marked points

Click each marked point in the graph. Record its input first and output second. These pairs become table rows.

content.prompt: Which three rows come from the marked points on the graph?
content.hint: Click each marked point and read the complete ordered-pair label. Do not reverse the coordinates.
content.explanation: The marked points are \((0,3)\), \((1,4)\), and \((2,9)\). A graph can therefore supply the rows for a regression table.

blocks.html:
Choose the model the data need

A model is the equation form used to describe the data.

  • Linear: a constant change over equal input steps.
  • Quadratic: a parabola, using \(y=ax^2+bx+c\).
  • Exponential: a constant multiplying factor over equal input steps.

Use the type named in the question when one is given.

content.prompt: The x-values increase by 1 while the y-values are 7, 14, 28, and 56. Which standard model should you select?
choices: Quadratic, because there are four points
Exponential, because each output is multiplied by 2
Custom, because the values are large
content.hint: Compare each output with the one before it. Are you adding a fixed amount or multiplying by a fixed factor?
content.explanation: Each output is twice the previous output, so the data fit a standard exponential model.

blocks.html:
Points, Table, Regression

  1. Find input-output pairs.
  2. Use Add Item (+) → Table and enter the pairs.
  3. Click the Regression button beside the table values.
  4. Select Linear, Quadratic, or Exponential and read the equation.

The button looks like a fitted line with scatterplot dots.

content.prompt: You entered four points and need a quadratic equation. What should you do next?
choices: Type \(y=ax^2+bx+c\) on a new line as a custom regression for all three letters.
Choose Linear from the regression options and adjust the coefficients by hand.
Delete the table and re-plot each of the four points separately.
Click the Regression button beside the table, then select Quadratic from its dropdown.
content.hint: The standard tool already contains the quadratic form. Use the table's Regression control.
content.explanation: Click the Regression button, then select Quadratic. Desmos fits \(y=ax^2+bx+c\) without requiring you to type it.

content.title: Guided practice: fit a line
content.instructions_html: Enter the shared points in a table. Click Regression and keep Linear. Read the equation.

feedback.success_message_html: Nice work! The line is fitted. Check it against \((0,9)\) before continuing.
feedback.retry_message_html: Not yet. Check the table rows, the regression row, and the model against the problem, then submit again.

targeted_hints.message_html: Reset the calculator, then enter all four points in a table.
The table does not hold the required rows yet. Re-check each value against the problem.
With the table filled, click the small regression button beside the table values (a line with four scatterplot dots).

feedback.solution_html: Table rows \((-1,11)\), \((0,9)\), \((2,5)\), \((4,1)\), then the Regression button with the model kept Linear.

figure.alt: A Desmos table with an arrow pointing to the Regression button beside it, shown as a fitted line with four scatterplot dots
figure.caption: The Regression button sits beside the table values.

content.prompt: Which linear equation should Desmos display for these data points?
content.solution:
Enter \((-1,11)\), \((0,9)\), \((2,5)\), and \((4,1)\) in a table and click the Regression button.
The points follow a line, so keep the model set to Linear.
Desmos displays the fitted equation directly: \(y=-2x+9\).
So the answer is choice B, \(y=-2x+9\).
content.hint: Read the equation beside the table. The output is 9 when the input is 0, and the outputs decrease as x increases.
content.explanation: The regression gives \(y=-2x+9\). It has a negative slope and passes through \((0,9)\).

blocks.html:
Read function notation as a pair

In \(g(t)=v\), \(t\) is the input and \(v\) is the output, so the point is \((t,v)\). The function may describe height after time, cost for a quantity, or another input-output relationship.

content.prompt: The function \(P(h)\) estimates a plant's height, in centimeters, \(h\) weeks after planting. Which quantity belongs in each Desmos table column?
choices: Left: weeks and centimeters mixed together; right: blank
Left: the function name \(P\); right: the letter \(h\)
content.hint: The phrase “h weeks after planting” names the input. The function estimates the output height.
content.explanation: Time \(h\) is the input on the left, and the estimated height \(P(h)\) is the output on the right.

shared_prompt.title: Medicine data
shared_prompt.html:
A function \(g(t)\) estimates the amount of medicine remaining, in milligrams, \(t\) hours after a dose. The problem states:

  • \(g(0)=96\)
  • \(g(1)=48\)
  • \(g(2)=24\)

blocks.html:
Translate the medicine statements

Use each time as the input and its medicine amount as the output. Then look at how the amount changes over equal time steps.

content.prompt: Which points should be entered in the Desmos table?
content.explanation: The inputs are 0, 1, and 2; their corresponding outputs are 96, 48, and 24.

content.title: Fit the function data
content.instructions_html: Enter the medicine points in a table. Click Regression and select Exponential. Translate the displayed input and output back to \(t\) and \(g(t)\).

feedback.success_message_html: Nice work! The exponential model is fitted. Translate \(x\) back to \(t\) and \(y\) to \(g(t)\).
feedback.retry_message_html: Not yet. Check the table rows, the regression row, and the model against the problem, then submit again.

targeted_hints.message_html: Reset the calculator and enter the three medicine data points in a table.
The table does not hold the required rows yet. Re-check each value against the problem.
With the table filled, click the small regression button beside the table values (a line with four scatterplot dots).

feedback.solution_html: Table rows \((0,96)\), \((1,48)\), \((2,24)\), then the Regression button with the model set to Exponential.

figure.alt: A Desmos table with an arrow pointing to the Regression button beside it, shown as a fitted line with four scatterplot dots
figure.caption: The Regression button sits beside the table values.

content.prompt: Which equation models the medicine data?
content.solution:
Enter \((0,96)\), \((1,48)\), and \((2,24)\) in a table and click the Regression button.
Each step multiplies the output by the same factor, so select Exponential from the model dropdown.
Desmos displays \(y=96(0.5)^x\); translate the roles back to the problem, where \(x\) stands for \(t\) and \(y\) stands for \(g(t)\).
So the answer is choice B, \(g(t)=96(0.5)^t\).
content.hint: The initial output is 96, and each one-hour increase multiplies the output by 0.5.
content.explanation: Desmos's \(y=96(0.5)^x\) becomes \(g(t)=96(0.5)^t\) in the problem's notation.

blocks.html:
Use the button for its supplied forms

The dropdown supplies linear, quadratic, and exponential models. If a problem requires a different form or directly asks for constants in a special form, use the custom-regression method taught separately.

content.prompt: Which requested model is directly covered by this standard-regression lesson?
content.hint: Use only the linear, standard quadratic, or exponential form supplied by the Regression dropdown.
content.explanation: \(y=a\cdot b^x\) is one of the standard models in this lesson. The other requests need a different workflow or custom form.

shared_prompt.title: Parabola data
shared_prompt.html: A question may tell you that a parabola has vertex \((2,-3)\) and passes through \((5,6)\).

blocks.html:
A vertex gives you useful extra information

A quadratic table needs enough information for three coefficients. When the question gives a vertex and one other point, symmetry can supply another table row.

Find the matching point

The vertex has x-coordinate 2. The point \((5,6)\) is 3 units to its right. Find the point 3 units to its left at the same height, then use both points with the vertex.

content.prompt: Which point is the reflection of \((5,6)\) across the line of symmetry?
content.hint: The known x-value is 3 units right of 2. Move 3 units left of 2 and keep the y-value 6.
content.explanation: Three units left of \(x=2\) is \(x=-1\), and the reflected point stays at height 6.

content.title: Use all three quadratic points
content.instructions_html: Enter \((2,-3),(5,6),(-1,6)\) in a table. Click Regression and select Quadratic. Read the standard-form equation.

feedback.success_message_html: Nice work! The quadratic is fitted through all three points.
feedback.retry_message_html: Not yet. Check the table rows, the regression row, and the model against the problem, then submit again.

targeted_hints.message_html: Reset the calculator and enter all three points, including the reflected one.
The table does not hold the required rows yet. Re-check each value against the problem.
With the table filled, click the small regression button beside the table values (a line with four scatterplot dots).

feedback.solution_html: Table rows \((2,-3)\), \((5,6)\), \((-1,6)\), then the Regression button with the model set to Quadratic.

figure.alt: A Desmos table with an arrow pointing to the Regression button beside it, shown as a fitted line with four scatterplot dots
figure.caption: The Regression button sits beside the table values.

content.hint: Read the displayed quadratic. As a quick check, substitute \(x=5\); the result must be \(6\).
content.explanation: \(y=x^2-4x+1\) gives \(y=-3\) at \(x=2\) and \(y=6\) at both symmetric inputs \(x=-1\) and \(x=5\).

blocks.html:
Return to the plant data

Try the opening question again. Choose the model the question asks for and find the requested coefficient.

content.hint: Use the times as inputs and the heights as outputs. Select the named model, then read the coefficient attached to the squared input.
content.solution:
Enter \((1,9.5),(3,13.5),(6,42),(8,76)\) in a table.
Click Regression and choose Quadratic.
The fitted equation is \(y=1.5x^2-4x+12\).
The coefficient of the squared input is \(a=1.5\).
content.explanation: You found \(a=1.5\). The table and Regression button built the quadratic, leaving you to read the coefficient the question wanted.

content.prompt: A word problem gives points and names the model it needs. What is the table-and-button routine, in order?
choices: Identify input-output points, enter them in a table, click Regression, keep the Linear model for every dataset, and translate the displayed equation back to the problem.
Identify input-output points, type a guessed equation, adjust its coefficients until the graph passes near the table's points, and report the closest version.
Enter the outputs in a table, click Regression, choose the appropriate standard model, and keep the displayed \(y_1\) and \(x_1\) letters in the final answer.
Identify input-output points, enter them in a table, click Regression, choose the appropriate standard model, and translate the displayed equation back to the problem.
content.explanation: You have it. That sequence handles points from tables, graphs, and word problems while letting the standard Regression tool build the equation.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.prompt: For a linear function \(h\), \(h(0)=12\), and \(h(x)\) decreases by \(3\) for each increase of \(1\) in \(x\). Which equation defines \(h\)?
content.explanation: The intercept is \(h(0)=12\) and the rate is \(-3\) per unit, so \(h(x)=-3x+12\). Entering the points \((0,12)\) and \((1,9)\) in a table and clicking Regression displays the same line.

content.prompt: A quadratic function f satisfies \(f(0)=1\), \(f(1)=4\), and \(f(2)=11\). What is the coefficient of \(x^2\) in its standard-form equation?
content.explanation: The points \((0,1),(1,4),(2,11)\) give \(f(x)=2x^2+x+1\), so the requested coefficient is 2.

content.html:
Points, Table, Regression

Keep input and output in order, then select the model the problem needs.
